text:
The first thing Miss Emily ever said to me was that I looked like someone who had been underpaid my whole life, and I laughed, because she was right, and because I was thirty-one years old, wearing a borrowed dress, standing at my own engagement party, and had been expecting opinions about the dress.

I had been a cashier for twelve years before I met Graham, at the Foodfair on Route 9, from the age of nineteen until the day I walked in with a man who was looking for beeswax and linen thread and was clearly embarrassed about both. Twelve years is a long time to be the same shape in the same place. You learn the codes. You learn which customers argue about the bananas before they reach the register. You learn that the deli counter smells like yesterday, that the paper towels come in two grades, that the private-label olive oil in the bulk bins is not worth the price of itself, and that the man at the bakery named Denny would, if everything went according to plan, be the last man I ever dated, because Denny and I had a plan, and the plan was simple, and it involved no estates and no opinions about anything.

Graham was not in my plan. He was in my register lane with a small paper bag, one beeswax block and a spool of thread, apologizing to the two people behind him for making them wait, which they had not been.

"Book restoration," he said, when I asked what the beeswax was for.

"Really?" I said, because I had no idea what beeswax was for, and I liked him immediately for the way he said it, like he was a little surprised by himself too.

He worked in a studio off the main street, restoring spines and covers, the kind of work that pays in patience. He told me he found the whole thing quietly miraculous, that a book could be held together for another hundred years if you were willing to sit still long enough. I told him I was good at sitting still. I had sat behind a register for twelve years.

We married in the spring, eight months later, and it was only at his mother's house, three weeks before the wedding, that I understood what had actually happened to me.

Graham had mentioned his mother the way other people mention the weather. Emily Marsh, he said, running her fingers along the spine of a sixteenth-century psalter. She runs a company. She's very good at it.

Everyone in the county had seen Miss Emily before. She had built Marsh Personnel out of one warehouse client and one truck, and now placed twenty thousand temporary workers across three states, and she had appeared on the local news in the winter of 2019 when she announced she was paying her temp workers overtime during the flu season and gotten called, by a man who had never paid anyone overtime in his life, a "compassionate capitalist." I had watched that interview at home and thought: there are people like her, and there are people like me, and she has a foundation named after her mother, and I have a name tag that says NELL.

Then Graham's mother came down the stairs of Graham's mother's house to meet me, and the two categories I had spent my whole life sorting people into came crashing together in the same room.

The house was in the hills above town, quiet the way big houses are quiet, hushed, as if the furniture were holding its breath. A woman named June brought us tea and did not meet my eyes. Graham sat me in a chair that was worth more than my rent, and the door at the top of the stairs opened, and Miss Emily came down, tall, straight-backed, silver at the temples, wearing a black suit and pearls the way other people wear gloves.

"So you're the one," she said. Not unkindly. Like a woman assessing a horse.

"I'm Nell," I said.

"Nell." She looked at me for a moment that lasted longer than was comfortable. "You look like someone who has been underpaid your whole life."

I have never been good at lying to people who can see through me, and I have never been good at lying in general, having spent twelve years telling people the exact truth about the price of things. "You're right," I said. "I was a cashier for twelve years. Eleven dollars an hour at the end of it."

"Twelve years," she said, and her face did something I had not expected, it opened, slightly, the way a door does when it recognizes a key. "Twelve years at a register is discipline. Most people are expensive, Nell. They want things they haven't earned and spend their lives resenting the people who have them. You want nothing. That's a problem you made for yourself, but it's a clean problem. I can live with clean."

She sat down, and for the next hour she did not ask about my childhood or my dreams. She asked how many registers I had worked in a day, whether the store ran its own shrinkage reports, who had trained me on the produce coding. I talked, and she listened with that terrible, attentive stillness, and when she was done she said, "Graham is a good boy. He's wasted on books. But you're not wasted on anything. Let's see what you do."

She gave me diamond earrings for my birthday, because the ones I wore were a mistake, but a charming one.

The wedding was Miss Emily's project. That was the word she used, at the caterer's tasting, where she insisted on attending in person because she had been to forty weddings in her life and most of them had been disasters. She paid for the venue, a stone hall on the river with a garden planted by someone who understood that trees take years, and the flowers, and the band, and the long tables where she sat me next to her daughter's friends from forty years ago, who treated me the way people treat a rescue dog they've just adopted: warmly, and with visible suspicion.

At the reception she stood up without notes. She told the story of the first person she had ever hired, a girl of seventeen who showed up at the warehouse with a bus transfer and shoes full of holes and no references at all, and whom she had kept anyway, because she watched her work the loading dock for an hour and saw that the girl wasted nothing, not time, not cardboard, not attention. That girl, Miss Emily said, now ran a division out of Columbus.

"I have never once regretted hiring a person," she said. "I regret not hiring more of them. Graham is the one person I have ever hired who refused to work for me, and I have spent his whole life deciding whether that makes him my best investment or my worst mistake." She looked at him across the room, and there was something in her face then that I have since learned to read as love, which in Miss Emily's language means ferocity aimed at a target she considers worth the ammunition. "But he married a woman who spent twelve years giving this town its groceries and never once took a single thing that wasn't hers." She turned to me. "Nell, you should know that I don't give things to people I don't intend to keep. I'm keeping you. Consider that the most expensive thing I've ever given away."

There were tears in the room, and I want to be honest that some of them were mine.

The first year of marriage was a series of small surrenders, each so gradual I only noticed it in retrospect. I learned that the house Graham and I rented above his studio was lovely, and that the word Miss Emily used for it was *charming*, which in her vocabulary meant *a place where things break*. I learned which fork to use, that the wine list was not a list but a hierarchy, and that our towels were the good grade, which I knew, because I had stocked both grades for years and could tell them apart by feel the way other people tell dogs apart. I learned to drive Graham's sensible car with a grace she approved of over the phone.

She took me shopping in the fall, on a Saturday morning, in a car that arrived without a driver, because she had decided I deserved one. She bought me a closet's worth of clothes in dark, clean colors, and while the bags were being filled she said, "You dress like a woman apologizing for the space she takes. It started at work, probably. Twelve years of keeping your hands visible and your voice small. Stop it. You're paid to exist here. Act like it."

I tried. I can tell you I tried, because I still apologize for bumping into doorframes, and one time I said sorry to a woman in the grocery aisle who had been pushed by me for half a second, and I felt the whole history of my life standing up behind me and saying, *that's who you are, Nell, and you can buy as many dresses as you like.*

What I did not tell anyone, and it took me longer to admit to myself than anything else, is that I liked parts of it. I liked that no one ever once told me to keep my voice small. I liked that when I started keeping a ledger of the household, because I found myself doing it, tallying what the studio spent, what the groceries cost, what Graham's materials were running him, Miss Emily called one evening and said, "You have the eye for waste. I've been looking for that eye in my own company for years." She asked me to come see the offices.

Marsh Personnel occupied a building downtown with floors of dispatchers and a conference room with my name on no plaque but on one calendar. Miss Emily walked me through it like a museum curator, explaining that at any given moment twenty thousand people worked under her, and that her job was not to exploit them, which she said with great precision, but to be the most honest employer in the state. "I have never fired anyone for being slow," she said. "I've fired people for being dishonest. Slowness I can train."

At the end of the visit she did something I have spent three years trying to classify. "If you ever want anything, Nell, you come to me. Not now. I'm not asking you to do anything. But I want you to understand that the door exists."

I said thank you. I meant it, and I also felt the weight of it, the way you feel the weight of a coat draped over your shoulders that you never agreed to wear.

Graham, when I told him, sat at his bench with a book open in front of him and was quiet for a long time. "She's not threatening you," he said finally. "She just loves people that way. If she loved you softly, you'd be dead in a year."

It was the truest thing anyone has ever said to me, and it made me love him a little more and fear his mother a little less, and I noticed that even those two feelings arrived dressed in her vocabulary.

Here is where I should say I was happy, and I was, in the ways a person can be happy while being slowly remade. But there is one more part of the story, and it's the part I keep coming back to, because it's the part where I lost something I hadn't known I still owned.

In my second year of marriage, I started taking Saturday shifts at the Foodfair. Not because I needed the money, which was the first thing Miss Emily would have asked, and the question she would have been right to ask. I went back because the register called to me, the way a river calls to a person who has lived beside it. The store had new management. A soft-spoken man named Alvarez hired me in an afternoon and said I was the best cashier he had ever seen, which I took as flattery and which was, I now suspect, the truth. I knew every code, every customer, every way the banana prices shifted before the sign changed.

By the following spring I was a keyholder. I wore the tag like the old one, like armor, like a small bright proof that I still existed in the world where I had been born.

Miss Emily found out the way Miss Emily finds out everything, which is to say she found out about it the way she found out about the price of steel and the flu rates in Ohio, by being the kind of person who knows things.

She didn't call. She came to dinner, which she did rarely, and poured herself wine with her own hands, which she also did rarely, and said, "I know about the supermarket."

I braced for fury. I had braced before, at the tasting, in the car, when she once told me my posture was "a betrayal of your own skeleton," and each time the fury had turned out to be a different animal wearing fury's clothes.

"They're paying you eleven dollars an hour," she said. "I looked it up. That's not a job. That's a crime against the people who hire you."

I told her it was my Saturday. I told her I loved it. I told her it was the only thing in my life I had ever been excellent at, and that I had never once taken a single thing that wasn't mine, and that the eleven dollars was mine, and I had earned it, and I was proud of it, and I said all of this in a voice I was only later able to recognize as the voice of a woman defending a treasure.

She looked at me for a long moment, and then she said, "I'm going to write to their regional office."

"I didn't ask you to fix it," I said.

She set her glass down. Then she picked it up again, poured me some too, and said, "I know you didn't. Asking is for people who might say no."

"Eleven dollars an hour is a crime," she went on. "I'll say that much and then stop, because it's yours to defend, and I respect people who defend their own things. I will say one other thing. There's a night shift at that store, and they aren't paying those people overtime either, and those people don't have me in their corner. I'm writing about them."

I wanted to argue that she wasn't in my corner either, exactly, but I had learned by then that Miss Emily's corner was the size of a state and the temperature was negotiable.

She never mentioned the supermarket again, except once, at a dinner a year later, when she asked how the Saturdays were going and I said fine and she said, "Eleven dollars. Still," and I said, "Still."

I kept the tag. I kept the register lane, the banana codes, the way the light comes through the loading doors on a Sunday morning. By every ledger in the world I was still underpaid, and I was still glad. I had never once taken a single thing that wasn't mine, and that included this.
